query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the in situ formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer during mechanical deformation is the key mediator that simultaneously enhances wear resistance and stabilizes passive films against corrosion. This dynamic nanostructuring reduces friction and wear by increasing grain boundary strengthening while promoting the formation and adherence of a protective oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy in its as-processed state featuring a relatively coarser grain structure and baseline passive film properties.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to combined cyclic mechanical loading and exposure to a corrosive environment (e.g., saline solution) that encourages dynamic surface restructuring.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under controlled mechanical wear (e.g., repeated sliding/impact) while immersed in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl) at room temperature. A matched control sample should experience only one of these stresses or be pre-treated to inhibit dynamic nanocrystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: The ultra-nanocrystalline, high-density grain boundary topography that forms on the surface due to dynamic amorphization during wear cycles.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical loading induces grain refinement at the surface, creating an ultra-fine near-surface layer that not only lowers friction and limits material removal (wear) but also provides abundant and stable nucleation sites for a protective oxide film. This passivation film is more adherent and resistant to breakdown, thereby reducing corrosion. The synergy of these effects governs the enhanced resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy lacking the dynamic ultra-nanostructured surface, the alloy under combined loading is expected to show significantly reduced wear rates and lower corrosion current density, reflecting improved wear and corrosion resistance. It is predicted that the combined degradation metrics (e.g., wear volume, friction coefficient, corrosion rate) will be reduced by a noticeable margin (potentially on the order of 30–50%), though the exact magnitude is context-dependent.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy with similar composition but either in a pre-treated condition that prevents dynamic nanocrystallization (for example, via an inhibitor coating) or tested under solely mechanical or solely corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: The prediction holds in environments where mechanical deformation is sufficient to induce dynamic surface nanocrystallization and where the corrosive medium is capable of forming a passive film on these refined grain boundaries. The effect may fail or be less pronounced when mechanical stresses are too low to trigger the nanocrystalline transformation or when the environment is so aggressive that any passivation film is quickly compromised despite the refined structure.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of the nano-layer formation on corrosion passivation stability and wear resistance is uncertain and likely varies with alloy composition, deformation mode, and corrosive species. Further detailed in situ characterization is required to fully quantify the interplay.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical bulk composition. For one set (Group A), allow the natural formation of the dynamic ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer under cyclic mechanical loading in a corrosive medium. For the matched baseline (Group B), inhibit surface grain refinement—for example, by a thermal treatment or a surface coating that prevents grain boundary movement—then subject them to the same testing conditions. Monitor both groups under identical sliding wear tests concurrently performed in a saline solution environment.
measurements: Passive film thickness and integrity (using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Group B (without the dynamic ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer) exhibits similar or superior wear and corrosion resistance (i.e., no statistically significant difference in wear volume, friction coefficient, and corrosion current density) compared to Group A, then the hypothesis that the dynamic formation of the surface nanocrystalline layer is the key mediator of improved combined performance is falsified.

Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding

Abstract: To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMo0.85 High-Entropy Alloy for Corrosion Resistance Coatings

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
